reverse_outline.summary: Chapter promise: how products, variants, identifiers and attributes are modeled, who owns each piece, and when a PIM is worth having.

Three key points: a product is four layered things with permanent identifiers; product data needs one owner per attribute; channels validate by their own rules and reject quietly, so syndication needs a feedback loop.
The three failure patterns the chapter addresses: Spaghetti Junction, Pulled Rug, Giant's Boots.
Hook: one jacket in 24 variants must reach many channels and languages, and a correction that lands in only one channel leaves buyers elsewhere misinformed.
Product data grows up scattered across systems and the copies drift on the first change; the remedy is an owner per field with channels as consumers.
Where the chapter sits in the order's journey: the product record with its SKU and GTIN precedes everything, changes slowest, and keys the price, discount and stock facts.
Roadmap of the chapter: the season-launch scene, what a product is, field ownership, the PIM picture, four arrangements with trade-offs and stages, practice, decision and failures.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Who Owns Which Field: Producers, Consumers and the System of Record ¶2

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶2

reverse_outline.summary: The data flows between systems each have different requirements (introduces the per-flow table).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Content flows tolerate delay but must be complete before publication.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶5

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶6
reverse_outline.summary: Bridge: three ownership rules satisfy these requirements.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶7
reverse_outline.summary: Rule 1: each attribute has one direction of flow from its single owner; a field editable in two places will diverge.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶8
reverse_outline.summary: Rule 2: publish complete products atomically on a schedule rather than field-by-field on change.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: How the Pieces Fit Together With a PIM ¶9
reverse_outline.summary: Rule 3: channel responses must return to the owner via a per-channel outbox, pre-validation and rejection tasks.
Arrangement 1 of four: the shop platform as the catalog, the right start for one channel and one language.
Arrangement 2: the ERP as product master, fine for identity and cost but poor for marketing content.
Arrangement 3: disciplined spreadsheets, which break down with the number of writers and readers rather than with size.
Arrangement 4: a PIM as system of record for content with ERP keeping identity and cost, right only under stated conditions.
A fifth option, full master data management, is deferred to the Group stage and another chapter.
Recommendation: a PIM is warranted once there is more than one producer and more than one consumer; below that it is overkill, above it drift costs more than the tool.
Two assumptions behind the recommendation: the ERP stays the item master, and one person has authority over all product content.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The fitting arrangement shifts with the merchant's scale stage (introduces the stage table).

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Across stages only identifier discipline stays constant; ownership changes once, when content gets its own system.
First documented point: platform variant caps force merchants to split products or pick another catalog model.
Evidence on variant limits at Shopify and commercetools, and the lasting damage of splitting products to fit a cap.
Second documented point: channels check incoming records against their own rules and may reject what looks complete at home.
Evidence of Google's and bol's concrete requirements, which change on the channel's schedule (the Pulled Rug).
Bridge: W3 is a bought PIM, read here as four steps with illustrative dates.
Step 1, ownership first: the attribute-level ownership table for the jacket, written before any vendor demo, including a controlled color list.
Step 2, one direction per field: ERP creates, PIM imports and publishes whole products, shop editor is read-only for unowned fields.
Step 3, syndication with a loop: rejections come back as tasks and a per-channel completeness score exposes gaps before launch.
Step 4, migrating one consumer at a time, with the initial load doubling as a reconciliation of conflicting copies.
The modest measurable results: no agency import days, no untranslated launch, one spelling of the color everywhere.
Bridge: even with ownership, product data fails quietly, so certain failures must be watched for deliberately.
Failure: silent channel rejection, detected by per-variant listing status and recovered as an owner task.
Failure: identifier drift (reused or malformed SKUs/GTINs), caught by cross-reference checks and fixed by retiring, not editing.
Failure: one product split into several, found by shared name without a group id and repaired by a mapped merge.
Failure: translations out of step with the corrected source, prevented by blocking on per-locale completeness.
Failure: a channel changes its rules or retires an API (the Pulled Rug), countered by a named changelog reader and mappings kept as data.
The common thread of the failures: any copy needs scheduled reconciliation against its system of record.

Conclusion callback to the uncorrected waterproof rating: stable identifiers, one owner per attribute and a route back from channels would have carried it, and a PIM is just a home for the latter two.
Established take-aways: the four-part product with permanent identifiers, asynchronous channel rejection, and no deletion of sold products.
Context-dependent take-aways: when the shop platform stops sufficing, what the ERP owns, where mappings live, and whether variant limits matter.
Author's synthesis: settle the ownership table before buying a PIM, and treat syndication as an integration with a rejection loop.
Eight diagnostic questions for the reader's own company on copies, edit rights, identifiers, attributes, rejections, launch time, rule changes and agent readiness.
Hand-off to the next chapter: price is the next product-related fact, with its own cadence, legal weight and many copies.

The introduction opens on a specific case, states a disputable claim and gives a roadmap; none of the five weak patterns applies.
The conclusion returns to the opening case, synthesizes, sorts the take-aways and hands off; it recaps body evidence but adds none, and the only new subject is the declared hand-off to pricing.

What to Take Away ¶1 states the three-part synthesis and the place of the PIM as the spec declares; the so-what is carried by 'That boundary, not revenue, is the test for a PIM' and 'a PIM bought without the table becomes a fifth copy with a login'.

What to Take Away ¶1 returns to the corrected waterproof rating and says what was missing (no owning system; the correction made in a system that only shows it). Two flow readers found the callback hard to square with the scene; that is recorded under flow_is_followable.

The intro reader predicted every section in order (scene, product model, ownership, PIM, four arrangements with trade-offs and stages, documentation, the decision, failures) and the evidence (the Kestrel & Pine example and documented channel and platform requirements).
The reader answers not to buy, gives the more-than-one-producer and more-than-one-consumer test, says the shop platform is the right catalog below it and names the Giant's Boots.

The reader names the missing single owning system with a one-way flow to the channels, places the correction in the system of record, and says the shop platform's editor should be read-only for the field.
The reader answers retire and reissue, map the old one for history, never correct in place or reuse, because orders, the warehouse and the connector are keyed on it.
